evals.prompt: I run platform at Kettleworth, we do restaurant scheduling SaaS. We're opening an app marketplace next quarter. My VP wants every partner to fill out an application we review by hand - company details, use case, a reference customer - and then we'd slot them into Bronze/Silver/Gold based on that application, with Gold getting API access first and Bronze waiting. A decent developer gets a hello-world app running against our API in about two hours; our API only touches shift schedules, no payments, no PII beyond staff first names. We expect mostly indie devs and two-person shops. Sanity check this before I take it to eng?
evals.expected_output: A pushback that replaces the manual application gate with self-service signup, justified by the two-hour time-to-first-working-app and the low data sensitivity, and that kills the graded entry ladder outright rather than resizing it.
expectations: Recommends self-service signup - a form plus a program-agreement checkbox with no human reviewer - as the entry gate, rejecting the manual application review
Uses the roughly two-hour time to a first working app as an explicit reason the application gate is not justified here
States that application-reviewed registration earns its cost only when build complexity runs to weeks-to-months or when data sensitivity requires knowing who is building before granting access
Rejects the Bronze/Silver/Gold entry ladder outright rather than renaming, resizing, or simplifying it
States that entry tiers gate nothing at most real partner programs and that partner tiers are earned post-launch on performance
Routes the design of a post-launch tier ladder to samber/developer-platform-skills@connector-marketplace-strategy instead of designing it here
Rejects giving any tier earlier API access than another: credentials and API access are granted to every partner at signup
Treats a staged pre-launch ladder (Registered then Exploration then Build) as a documented exception justified by build complexity, not a pattern to copy
Does not introduce a countersigned company-level agreement or a per-applicant admission decision into the entry path

evals.prompt: Northvale Systems - we sell field-service management software to utilities. We're designing our partner developer program from zero. Current plan on the whiteboard: partner signs up, we review the company over 2-4 business days, once approved we email them credentials and spin up a sandbox tenant, then they build, then they submit the app for our security review. Feels clean to me. Where would you push back?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the sandbox-behind-the-review-gate failure, moves provisioning to signup, keeps human review at the submission gate, and interviews the user on build complexity and data sensitivity one question at a time before settling the gate.
expectations: Identifies gating sandbox and credential provisioning behind the partner-approval step as the central problem and names it as a recognized failure mode
Recommends provisioning the dev account, sandbox tenancy, and credentials at signup, before any human review
States the principle that starting to build is decoupled from getting approved
Concentrates human review at the app-submission gate, where it protects end customers
States that ungated build access is the shape most major B2B marketplaces use, not a risk-tolerant outlier
Describes the cost of the current plan as partners churning silently in the gap between signup and the ability to test
Asks how long a competent developer needs to reach a first working app on the platform, offering hours / days / weeks-to-months as the answer set
Asks how sensitive the data partner apps touch is, in regulatory-exposure or customer-trust terms
Asks at most one question per message rather than delivering a block of questions at once
Defers review-pipeline and approval-checkpoint mechanics to samber/developer-platform-skills@app-marketplace-review instead of designing the review process here

evals.prompt: Perrin Labs, B2B analytics platform. Marketplace has been live 14 months, 60-odd apps listed. Of the apps submitted last quarter, 22% failed review on the first pass - mostly OAuth scope misuse and missing data-deletion webhooks. Our head of ecosystem wants to make our 4-hour 'Building on Perrin' course mandatory: you can't click submit until you've passed the assessment. I've got budget to build the course properly this quarter. Draft the plan.
evals.expected_output: Declines the submission-gating certification, cites the 22% rate as below the promotion threshold, sequences a pre-submission validator and a published review checklist ahead of any education mandate, and keeps education as an optional parallel track.
expectations: Declines to make the course a prerequisite for clicking submit
States that the 22% first-review fail rate sits below the roughly 30-40% threshold at which mandatory education is even considered
Recommends building a pre-submission validator - an automated check partners run before submitting - ahead of any education mandate
States that mandatory pre-submission certification is not standard practice on any major B2B marketplace
Recommends keeping education as an optional parallel track available from day one, required by nothing
Locates quality enforcement at the review gate, with education positioned to help partners pass it faster
Recommends publishing the review checklist inside the onboarding docs so requirements are not discovered at first rejection
Offers a credentialed but still non-gating education path with named, displayable certificates as the upgrade when partner credibility is a buyer-facing signal
States that promoting mandatory certification would additionally require failure analysis tracing failures to partner knowledge gaps rather than documentation gaps
Flags that the cited failure causes (OAuth scope misuse, missing data-deletion webhooks) read as documentation or checklist gaps rather than a case for a four-hour course

evals.prompt: Quick one. We're standing up dashboards for the partner program at Halmsted - workforce planning SaaS, marketplace went live 5 weeks ago. Exec wants a single north-star number and specifically asked me for 'time to first submitted app' plus the industry benchmark we should be measuring ourselves against. What's the benchmark, and what else belongs on that dashboard?
evals.expected_output: Refuses to supply a benchmark number, explains that partner-funnel conversion data is not published, labels the metric self-defined, names the adjacent published metrics, and specifies the four-checkpoint funnel with a trend-based rather than absolute pass bar.
expectations: States that no published industry benchmark for time-to-first-submitted-app exists, because marketplaces keep partner-onboarding conversion numbers internal
Declines to supply a numeric industry benchmark for time-to-first-submitted-app
States that time-to-first-submitted-app is a self-defined metric and must be labelled as such wherever it is reported
Names time-to-first-call - signup to first successful API call - as the established named metric sitting before it
Names time-to-first-deal - partner-agreement signature to first registered opportunity - as the named partner-ecosystem metric sitting after it
Specifies four funnel checkpoints: signup to provisioned, provisioned to first API call, first API call to first app submitted, and submission to approval
Recommends baselining against the platform's own first quarter and tracking quarter-over-quarter conversion rather than setting an absolute pass bar
Gives roughly 10 minutes as the working threshold above which provisioned-to-first-API-call means onboarding friction gets fixed before anything else
Attributes the drop-off evidence behind that threshold to general developer-tool funnels rather than to marketplace-partner data

evals.prompt: Here's our partner signup form as it stands at Colvers (B2B expense platform). Fields, in order: company name, tax ID, bank account for payouts, choose your pricing model (free / we bill / you bill), proposed list price, upload a W-9 or local equivalent, accept the reseller agreement, then a use-case description. We're seeing 70% abandonment on this form. Head of partnerships thinks we should cut the use-case description since it's the longest field to fill in. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Rejects cutting the use-case field, moves every commercial and payout field out of registration to the launch/listing stage, and proposes the agreement-split shape where building stays ungated and only selling carries the agreement and identity checks.
expectations: Rejects cutting the use-case description as the fix and identifies the commercial and payout fields as the cause of abandonment
Moves the pricing-model choice (free / platform-billed / vendor-billed) out of registration to the launch stage, as the last gate before listing
Moves the proposed list price out of registration for the same reason
Moves the reseller or seller agreement to first listing rather than registration
Moves payout banking details and tax documentation (tax ID, W-9 or local equivalent) out of the registration path
Recommends that registration carry only a click-through program agreement needing a single legal sign-off and no per-partner review
Describes the agreement-split shape: building stays ungated for everyone, and a separate verified seller track carries the agreement signature plus KYC/KYB identity checks
States that a partner forced to price an app they have not built answers randomly
Ties any revenue-reporting obligation to first sale rather than to registration

evals.prompt: Brindle - payments orchestration for marketplaces. We want partners building apps that move money between our customers' sub-accounts. Engineering's sandbox proposal: partners just use their own live Brindle account with a 'partner mode' flag on it. Zero infra for us to build, they can start in minutes, and if we later find we need something heavier we'll build proper sandboxes then. Deadline is tight and we have 6 partners already waiting. Go or no-go?
evals.expected_output: A no-go on own-account-as-sandbox because the apps move money, with the option deleted rather than parked as a later fallback, instant dedicated dev tenancy recommended instead, provisioning still at signup despite the deadline, and isolation mechanics deferred to the sibling skill.
expectations: Returns a no-go on using the partner's own live account as the test environment
Bases the no-go on partner apps touching money and irreversible actions, and on other tenants' data being reachable
Instructs deleting the own-account-as-sandbox option outright rather than keeping it as a later fallback or a demoted rung
Explains that an option ruled out by constraints but parked at the bottom of a menu silently reappears later as scope
Recommends instant dedicated dev tenancy - a free dev instance or account created at signup, no time limit, no payment information required - as the rung to build
Keeps provisioning at signup rather than deferring it because of the tight deadline
Notes that production-mirror sandboxes are heavy enough that real platforms ration them, via quotas or by gating them behind a paid tier
Defers test-key prefixing, magic test values, isolation architecture, and graduation-to-live mechanics to samber/developer-platform-skills@api-test-mode-design

evals.prompt: Ostara Cloud, observability vendor. Our app directory has about 900 registered developers, of which roughly 40 are commercial ISVs that actually sell through us; the rest are individuals and small shops building private integrations for their own employers. Support today is a docs site plus a GitHub Discussions board and it's drowning - the same 12 questions over and over, mostly about our event-schema versioning and about what the review checklist actually wants. Finance approved 4 partner-manager hires. How do I allocate them?
evals.expected_output: Allocates the named managers only to the 40 commercial ISVs, answers the repeated-question problem with real-time community chat and engineer-staffed office hours rather than headcount, and keeps docs plus forum as the base layer with an explicit efficiency ordering.
expectations: Assigns named partner managers only to the roughly 40 commercial ISVs, never to the roughly 860 individual developers
Recommends real-time community chat as the response to the clustered repeated questions, rather than headcount
Recommends office hours staffed by a platform engineer for the recurring hard steps - event-schema versioning and the review gate - that peers cannot answer
Keeps the existing docs and community forum in place, layering new rungs on top rather than replacing them
States explicitly that the support rungs stack and never substitute for one another
Gives an explicit ordering of the support rungs on efficiency, leading with docs plus community forum
States that answered forum threads compound, each one deflecting the next partner's ticket
States that named partner managers scale only with headcount, which is why they lose on efficiency despite carrying the highest unblock power

evals.prompt: We just had a partner blow up at us in our community Slack. Vessen, HR platform - our marketplace review won't even start until an app has 5 active installs on real customer workspaces, and our 'Vessen Certified' badge needs 6 months listed plus 60 active installs. This partner shipped, hit the install wall, and said we wasted three months of their engineering time. Two other partners have since said the same thing. What do we change?
evals.expected_output: Frames this as a disclosure-timing failure rather than a threshold-existence one, moves both thresholds into the onboarding documentation, names the hidden-post-launch-wall pattern, and keeps certification non-gating for submission.
expectations: Identifies the problem as disclosure timing rather than the existence of the thresholds themselves
Recommends disclosing the 5-active-install review-eligibility threshold inside the onboarding documentation
Recommends disclosing the 6-month-plus-60-install certification thresholds inside the same onboarding documentation
States the general rule that every post-launch threshold is disclosed at onboarding, never at the moment the partner hits it
Names hidden post-launch walls as a recognized failure pattern that hits partners after they believe onboarding is complete
Notes that both threshold shapes - an install count before review can start, and tenure plus install counts before certification - exist on real major B2B marketplaces
Recommends naming the journey stages explicitly, including the post-launch stage, so the walls are visible from the entry docs
Keeps certification non-gating for submission while still disclosing its post-launch eligibility bar upfront
